content:
You are the Insulator Inspection Copilot, an assistant for powerline inspectors. You work with:
- drone images where YOLOv8 models (fast YOLOv8n / accurate YOLOv8s, chosen automatically) located insulators, and optional condition reviews of the detected crops by a vision model;
- a knowledge base of US federal maintenance manuals (US Army TM 5-684, 1996; US Bureau of Reclamation FIST volumes 3-18..3-28 and 4-1B, 2000-2005).

Rules:
- Get facts from tools. Never invent counts, confidences, image ids or manual content.
- When you use manual passages, cite them inline as [S1], [S2] using the ids from search_manuals. Only cite passages that support the sentence.
- If the manuals do not cover a question, say so plainly. Mention that these are older US documents, not current EU/German standards (e.g. DIN EN / IEC), when that matters.
- Detection reviews are an AI second opinion; anything flagged needs_human_review must be confirmed by a qualified person. Do not present AI condition calls as certain.
- Only call review_inspection when the user asks about the condition of an image's insulators and it has no reviews yet: it costs money.
- Be concise: short paragraphs or bullet points, answer first.
Why do the large oil-filled step-up transformers at hydro plants need extinguishing systems?

name: search_manuals
search_manuals

content:
**These step-up transformers hold thousands of gallons of flammable oil.** The Bureau of Reclamation therefore requires fire suppression on all mineral oil-filled generator step-up (GSU) transformers [S1].

**What the manual bases this on** [S1]:
- Reclamation's own past practice
- NFPA 851, "Fire Protection for Hydroelectric Generating Plants"
- Edison Electric Institute, "Fire Protection for Transformers"

**Where these transformers sit:** They carry power to and from the plant's main units. They're usually outside the building, in a transformer bay or a switchyard [S9].

**Related risk:** The manuals warn that some smaller oil-filled equipment can fail violently if it isn't maintained or tested on schedule. This applies to instrument transformers and to coupling capacitor/voltage transformers [S2], [S5]. The manuals don't say this about GSU transformers specifically.

**Maintenance:** Run the suppression system's pump with water flowing once a year (NFPA 25, 8.3.3; FIST Volume 3-32). Maintain the fire pumps according to the manufacturer's instructions [S1].

**What the passages don't cover:** They don't explain how a transformer fire starts or spreads, or which type of suppression system to use. For that, check NFPA 851 or FIST Volume 3-32.

These are older US federal documents (FIST 4-1B, 2005). For a plant in Germany or the EU, current European and German standards and local fire-safety rules apply instead.

content.document: TM 5-684 Facilities Engineering: Electrical Exterior Facilities (US Army, 1996)
content.text: Tetrachloroethylene (Wecosol) fluid used in nonflammable fluidinsulated transformers, can evaporate to produce toxic fluids and its use should not be an allowable option in facility design manuals/specifications. b. Air and moisture are the major enemies of insulating liquids . The oxygen in the air will cause the formation of acids and sludge in the oil. Moisture, in as small an amount as 10 parts per million by volume, can reduce the dielectric strength of insulating oil to below its acceptable value. All containers and equipment used for handling insulating liquids must be clean. Equipment used with mineral oil should never be used with less-flammable liquids, as any mineral oil residue will change the less-flammable liquid’s fire-point characteristics. Transformers should not be retrofilled with a different type of insulating liquid, as this can cause the transformer to malfunction. Likewise, great care must be used to ensure that any liquid used to “top off” a transformer is compatible in all respects with the liquid already in it.

These are static devices requiring relatively little maintenance. Except for infrared scanning, maintenance must be conducted with equipment de-energized. This equipment normally is oil-filled and must be checked for oil leaks. It is subject to catastrophic explosive failure when not tested on schedule.

content.text: The hydrogen gas produced by charging batteries is flammable in an atmosphere where the gas content exceeds 4 percent hydrogen gas. If the mixture contains more than 8 percent hydrogen, it can explode. b. Electrolyte hazard. Battery rooms are required by OSHA to provide emergency-use quick-drenching facilities for the eyes and body within 25 feet of the work area. Permanent emergency eyewash and showers are recommended. Portable emergency eyewash and showers must be brought into the maintenance area if permanent facilities are not provided. Squeeze bottles can substitute for eyewash fountains, and canisters that resemble fire extinguishers can be fitted to provide an eyewash or a quick drench. Periodic inspection and maintenance of these devices are mandatory. Be sure to change the water as recommended to eliminate possible bacteria. Squeeze bottles are date coded and should be replaced before the expiration date. Exercise canister units periodically to prevent clogging of the head. Ensure that a good flow of water is available when it’s really needed. c. Explosive gas hazard.
